setup.zh: 开春，舅舅从县城来，念了一张告示：沉鼎观开山门，录为弟子者，家里每年五两银子。他刚念到「沉鼎」，你胸口的木牌烫得像一块炭。
setup.en: In spring Uncle comes from the county town and reads out a notice: Chending Temple opens its gate, and a disciple's family gets five taels a year. At the words "Chending" the token at your chest burns like a coal.

recap.zh: 舅舅带来了沉鼎观开山门的告示；他念到「沉鼎」，木牌烫得像炭——你决定去。开春以后，那一缕热卡在心口底下，账本末页的「下」字一直空着。
recap.en: Uncle brought the notice that Chending Temple would open its gate; at "Chending" the token burned like a coal — and you decided to go. After spring the thread of warmth stuck under your heart, and the *down* on the ledger's last page stayed bare.

zh: 舅舅：簇新的青布长衫，二斤肉，一包红糖。
en: Uncle: a brand-new blue gown, two jin of meat, a packet of brown sugar.
"…present themselves for trial at the foot of Chending Mountain."
Between your fingers, a thread of silver light.

story.zh:
开了春，二月里，蒙山脚下的县城城门口，贴出了一张告示。

三月初三，上巳，舅舅来了。舅舅是小满他娘的亲弟弟，在县城济世堂做账房，是沈家这一门亲戚里唯一「出息了」的人。他穿一身簇新的青布长衫，提着二斤肉、一包红糖，站在那扇装歪了的门口，拿袖子掩着鼻子，咳了一声。

他爹慌慌张张地拿袖子擦炕沿，擦了三遍，才请他坐。舅舅看了看屋顶，看了看墙角接水的那一排盆——十七个，整整齐齐，像一队站岗的兵——又看了看姐夫的膝盖，叹了口气：「姐，你这日子……」小满他娘道：「挺好。」「屋顶都漏成这样了——」「通风。」

舅舅张了张嘴，压低了声音：「姐，你当年要是听爹的话——」他娘道：「吃饭。」舅舅便闭上了嘴。小满心里一动：外公的话，是什么话？他看看他娘，她正低头给舅舅盛饭，盛得满满的；他爹低着头，一下一下地揉膝盖，揉得很用力。

吃饭的时候，舅舅从怀里摸出一张纸：「县城贴的告示。我给你们抄了一份。」清了清嗓子，念道：「**沉鼎观**，三年一开山门，收徒。凡十二至十六岁、身家清白者，皆可于九月初九，赴泗水沉鼎山下应试。录为弟子者，其家每岁由观中发给白银五两——」

他刚念到「沉鼎」两个字，小满胸口的木牌登时烫得像一块刚从灶膛里扒出来的炭，烫得他「嗷——！」的一声从凳子上蹦起来，一口饭，不偏不倚，全喷在了舅舅脸上。

没有人看见，小满捂在胸口的手指缝里，漏出了一线银光。木牌上那条银色的尾巴，不再一明一暗了，它亮着，一直亮着，像一个在梦里找了很久很久的人，终于听见了自己要找的那个名字。

他娘问道：「五两银子？」「一年五两。」他爹放下了筷子。沈家一年交马家的租，加上山风钱，加上这个钱那个钱，也不过三两。舅舅又压低了声音：「还有。家里有孩子进了仙门的——马家，不敢收租。」屋里静了。隔了一会儿，舅舅道：「姐。二十年前，我也去过。」

「那年我十四。三百级石阶，要在一炷香里走完。我爬到一百七十级，腿就动不了了。我在那儿坐了一炷香，看着别人一个一个从我身边走过去。然后我就下山了，去济世堂学打算盘。」他说这话的时候，眼睛看着桌上那碗饭，声音平得像在念账本上的一行字。小满他娘轻轻地道：「上回是一百六十级。」

舅舅的脸登时红得跟他提来的那二斤肉一个颜色：「每年都在长嘛！」小满憋不住了，问道：「舅舅，你见过仙人吗？」舅舅的神色登时郑重起来：「见过。前年冬天，济世堂来过一个穿灰袍的，走路没声儿，买了三两当归，我要找他钱，他摆摆手：不必。坐了十八年柜台，头一回有人跟我说不必。」舅舅转过头来，看着他：「你娘识字，你随她，脑子比我活。你爹打猎，你随他，腿脚比我稳。去试试。进不去，也不亏什么。进去了——」他没说完，看了一眼姐夫的膝盖，又看了一眼墙角那一排盆，便低下头吃饭了。
story.en:
When spring came, in the second month, a notice went up at the gate of the county town at the foot of Mount Meng.

On the third of the third month, the Shangsi festival, his uncle came. His uncle was his mother's own younger brother, bookkeeper at the Jishi Hall in the county town, the one relative in the Shen family who had "made something of himself". He wore a brand-new blue cloth gown and carried two catties of meat and a packet of brown sugar, and stood at the crooked door, sleeve over his nose, and coughed.

Xiaoman's father hurriedly wiped the edge of the kang with his sleeve three times before asking him to sit. His uncle looked at the roof, at the row of basins in the corner catching drips — seventeen, lined up neat as a squad of sentries — at his brother-in-law's knee, and sighed. "Sister, this life of yours…" Xiaoman's mother said, "It's fine." "The roof's leaking like this —" "Ventilation."

His uncle opened his mouth and lowered his voice. "Sister, if you'd listened to Father back then —" His mother said, "Eat." His uncle shut his mouth. Xiaoman was struck: Grandfather's words — what words? He looked at his mother; she had her head down, dishing rice for his uncle, piling the bowl high; his father had his head down too, rubbing his knee over and over, very hard.

Over the meal his uncle took a sheet of paper from his coat. "A notice posted in the county town. I copied it out for you." He cleared his throat and read: "**Chending Temple** opens its mountain gate once every three years to take disciples. All between twelve and sixteen years of age, of clean family, may present themselves for trial at the foot of Chending Mountain on the Si River on the ninth day of the ninth month. For those enrolled as disciples, the Temple will grant their family five taels of silver each year —"

The moment he read the word *Chending*, the token at Xiaoman's chest burned like a coal just raked from the stove, so hot that Xiaoman leapt off his stool with a yelp — and a mouthful of rice went, squarely, all over his uncle's face.

Nobody saw the thread of silver light leaking between the fingers Xiaoman pressed to his chest. The silver tail on the token no longer went bright and dim; it was lit and stayed lit, like someone who has searched a long, long time in a dream and at last heard the very name they were looking for.

His mother asked, "Five taels of silver?" "Five taels a year." His father put down his chopsticks. The Shens' rent to the Mas, plus the mountain-wind money, plus this money and that, came to no more than three taels a year. His uncle lowered his voice again. "And. A family with a child who's got into an immortal sect — the Mas daren't take rent from them." The room went quiet. After a while his uncle said, "Sister. Twenty years ago, I went too."

"I was fourteen. Three hundred stone steps, to be climbed within one stick of incense. I got to step one hundred and seventy, and my legs wouldn't move. I sat there the length of a stick of incense, watching others walk past me one by one. Then I came down the mountain and went to the Jishi Hall to learn the abacus." As he said it his eyes were on the bowl of rice, his voice flat as reading out a line of a ledger. Xiaoman's mother said softly, "Last time it was a hundred and sixty."

Uncle's face went as red as the two jin of meat he'd brought. "It grows every year!" Xiaoman couldn't hold it in. "Uncle, have you ever seen an immortal?" Uncle's face turned grave at once. "I have. Winter before last, a man in a grey robe came into the Jishi Hall — walked without a sound, bought three ounces of angelica root; I went to give him his change, and he waved his hand: no need. Eighteen years behind that counter, and the first time anyone ever told me no need." Uncle turned to look at him. "Your mother can read — you take after her, your head's quicker than mine. Your father hunts — you take after him, your legs are steadier than mine. Go and try. If you don't get in, you've lost nothing. If you get in —" He didn't finish; he glanced at his brother-in-law's knee, then at the row of basins in the corner, and lowered his head to his rice.

exits.means: decides to go to the temple trials

story.zh:
那天夜里，小满躺在炕上，一笔一笔地算账。五两银子，一年。他爹，再也不用拖着那条腿进深山；马三的短棍，再也敲不到沈家的门框；那件棉袄，今年冬天便有了，袖子不短，手腕不冻。然后，是另一笔账。他把木牌从衣领里掏出来，贴在耳朵边上听。它亮着，从晌午舅舅念告示的时候亮起来，一刻也没暗过。「……本王在找一个地方……一个名字……等你听见了，本王会知道的。」他听见了。他对着黑暗，小声说道：「好。我去。」木牌暖了一下。

他娘在账上「红糖一包，舅舅给」底下，添了一行：

三月初三。满，说要去。

舅舅是第二天一早走的。走出村口半里地，路边草垛后头钻出一个红鼻头的小姑娘，冲他鞠了一躬：「舅舅好。」舅舅吓了一跳：「我不是你舅舅。」「你是小满的舅舅。小满的舅舅，就是舅舅。」舅舅觉得这话有几分道理。小姑娘只问了一句：「考仙门，考不考算账？」舅舅上下打量了她一番，又问了她几句，她答得又快又清楚。舅舅便笑了，从怀里摸出一本济世堂用剩的空账簿，巴掌大小，蓝布面儿，递给了她。这件事，小满不知道。

那天夜里，他娘把竹简翻到了最后一片，念到「筑基」两个字，手指停住了，停了很久。「筑基，」她道，「就是盖房子，先打地基。这上头说，一百天。」她把竹简卷上，又道：「你外公说，人这一辈子，得往上走。我说，往上走的人够多了，山脚下总得有人把灶烧着。」她吹灭了灯。小满在黑地里掰着指头算：一百天。离九月初九，一百八十三日。够筑一回，还富余八十三天。这笔账，他算错了。

开春以后，那一缕热随着那口气往下沉，沉过胸口，到了心口底下，便停住了，再往下，怎么送也送不动，像一只水桶卡在了半截井绳上。一卡卡了一春一夏。他娘账本最末一页的「下」字，一直空着。
story.en:
That night Xiaoman lay on the kang reckoning the accounts entry by entry. Five taels of silver, every year. His father would never again have to drag that leg into the deep hills; Ma San's club would never again rap at the Shens' door-frame; and that padded jacket would be hers this very winter, sleeves long enough, wrists not frozen. Then there was the other account. He took the token out of his collar and held it to his ear. It was lit — lit since noon, when Uncle read the notice, and not dim for a moment since. *…This king is looking for a place… a name… when you hear it, this king will know.* He had heard it. He said softly into the dark, "All right. I'll go." The token warmed once.

Under "Brown sugar, one packet, from Uncle" his mother added a line:

Third month, third. Man: says he'll go.

Uncle left first thing the next morning. Half a li out of the village a red-nosed little girl popped out from behind a haystack and bowed to him. "Hello, Uncle." Uncle jumped. "I'm not your uncle." "You're Xiaoman's uncle. Xiaoman's uncle is Uncle." Uncle felt there was some sense in that. The little girl asked only one thing: "The immortals' exam — does it test accounts?" Uncle looked her up and down, asked her a few questions, and she answered fast and clear. Uncle laughed, took from his jacket a blank account book left over from the Jishi Hall, palm-sized, blue cloth cover, and gave it to her. Xiaoman didn't know about this.

That night his mother turned the scroll to its last slip; at the words "build the foundation" her finger stopped, and stayed a long time. "Building the foundation," she said, "is like building a house — first you lay the footings. It says here, a hundred days." She rolled up the scroll and said, "Your grandfather said, in this life a man must climb. I said, there are enough people climbing; somebody at the foot of the mountain has to keep the stove lit." She blew out the lamp. In the dark Xiaoman counted on his fingers: a hundred days. To the ninth of the ninth month, a hundred and eighty-three days. Enough to build it once, with eighty-three days to spare. He'd got that sum wrong.

After spring came, that thread of warmth sank with the breath, past the chest, and under his heart it stopped; further down, push as he might, it wouldn't go, like a bucket stuck halfway down a well rope. Stuck there it stayed, all spring and summer. The character *down* on the last page of his mother's ledger stayed bare.

exits.means: hesitates, decides not to go yet, waits

story.zh:
那天夜里，小满躺在炕上，对着黑暗，小声道：「不去……家里离不开我。再等三年。」

胸口的木牌，一下子凉了。那条亮了一整晚的尾巴，暗了下去——一明，一暗，一明——暗下去的那一下，比平时长。

他睁着眼睛躺到天亮。隔着一道布帘，他爹咳了半夜。
story.en:
That night Xiaoman lay on the kang and said softly into the dark: "I won't go… home can't do without me. Wait another three years."

The token at his chest went cold at once. The tail that had been lit all evening dimmed — bright, dim, bright — and the dim lasted longer than usual.

He lay with his eyes open till dawn. Through the cloth curtain his father coughed half the night.
